title: From arrest to appeal
blurb: The adult criminal process in order, from the first report to what happens after sentence.
closing: At every stage someone holds discretion (police, prosecutors, magistrates, juries, judges), and each stage has a check on it. That is why the Crime topic keeps returning to the tension between community interests and individual rights.

title: Powers against rights
blurb: Why every police power in the investigation process is paired with a protection for the suspect.
closing: Police need powers to detect crime, but evidence obtained improperly can be excluded. The law is balancing the truth of what happened against the integrity of the process.

title: From purposes to penalties
blurb: How a court moves from the purposes of punishment to a sentence, and what comes after.
closing: The same offence can be sentenced differently depending on which purpose is given the most weight. Alternatives such as circle sentencing and post-sentence regimes sit at opposite ends of the same debate.

title: A young offender's journey
blurb: What changes when the person questioned, charged or sentenced is a child.
closing: Every step has a child-specific version: a minimum age, extra protections when questioned, ways to stay out of court, a specialist court and different penalties.

title: From treaty to Australian law
blurb: Why signing an international treaty does not, by itself, give Australians an enforceable right.
closing: Rights in a treaty bind Australia internationally, but they only become enforceable in Australian courts when parliament legislates, using a power the Constitution gives it.

title: Pressure without power
blurb: How human rights are promoted internationally when no body can simply override a state.
closing: Where legal enforcement is limited, NGOs and the media supply the scrutiny that makes states comply. This is the legal v non-legal response pattern examiners ask about.

title: The Charter of Rights debate
blurb: The gaps in Australia's protections and the arguments about closing them.
closing: Statute and common law protect some rights piecemeal. A charter would add a single framework, at the cost of shifting power from parliament to the courts.

title: Family breakdown
blurb: From the end of a relationship to the resolution of parenting and property.
closing: Separation raises two questions (children and property), which the law steers through courts and dispute resolution, with cooperation preferred over conflict.

title: Protecting children from harm
blurb: How family violence and child protection law cut across parenting orders.
closing: Parents have rights and responsibilities, but a child's safety can override them. The law balances family autonomy against state intervention.

title: Buying, renting and disputes
blurb: What happens when securing shelter goes wrong and where a person can turn.
closing: Most shelter disputes are decided in a tribunal or settled by ADR. The roles of NGOs and government bodies fill the gaps between a right on paper and a remedy in practice.

title: From a right to shelter to social housing
blurb: How the international right to shelter becomes (or fails to become) a roof.
closing: Governments accept an obligation to provide shelter, but affordability pressures and homelessness show how far that obligation is met in practice.

title: From bill to binding rule
blurb: How Australian law is made and interpreted (Year 11).
closing: Parliament makes statutes and may delegate detail. Courts then interpret and apply them within a hierarchy, creating precedent that guides later cases.

title: How reform happens
blurb: The path from public concern to a changed law and its limits (Year 11).
closing: Informal pressure builds political will, formal processes produce a bill, and the outcome is judged by its benefits and its limitations.

title: Mabo to native title
blurb: The first case study of law reform (Year 11).
closing: Judicial decisions and legislation changed the law in turn. The result recognised rights but left significant limitations.

title: Disputes with the state
blurb: Where a person can turn when the government is the other party (Year 11).
closing: Remedies range from NGO and media pressure to formal review, an Ombudsman, and, for systemic failures, a royal commission.

title: Procedural fairness to the criminal trial
blurb: A Year 11 principle that becomes an HSC protection.
closing: A fair hearing and no bias in Year 11 become the adversary system, legal representation and the burden of proof in the criminal trial.

title: From international law to international crime
blurb: How state sovereignty shapes what the world can do about the worst crimes.
closing: International courts and tribunals depend on states cooperating, so the debate about sovereignty runs through both Crime and Human Rights.
